models.purpose: set a baseline for water access from income per person and population growth alone
models.summary: A two-predictor line fitted on 212 countries. Income per person raises access and population growth lowers it, and the line explains 43.7 percent of the variance.

gross domestic product per person, the proxy for ability to meet demand
annual population growth, the proxy for rising demand

locate the limits of the technique

details: every fit starts from the 2012 cross-section

parameter_estimation.method: ordinary least squares in R on 212 countries

steps: read off the slopes and the fit
algorithm.convergence_criteria: both predictors are significant and the adjusted R-squared is reported

assumptions: income per person proxies for the ability to meet it

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: the line, the adjusted R-squared and both p-values are printed

models.purpose: turn a published climate projection into a yearly loss of water access
models.summary: A reported three degree rise by the 2080s and a ten percent loss of supply are spread evenly over the years, giving a yearly loss that accumulates to 2.68 percentage points by 2031.

variables.definition: the yearly warming implied by a three degree rise by the 2080s
the yearly loss of water access implied by a ten percent supply loss
the accumulated warming from 2013 to 2031
the accumulated loss of water access by 2031

governing_equations.label: climate
governing_equations.purpose: the linear climate correction: warming and access loss per year, accumulated to 2031

equation_status.reason: displayed and read from the text layer

objectives: correct the forecast for a warming the regression cannot see
constraints: both warming and supply loss are linear in time

details: every fit starts from the 2012 cross-section

parameter_estimation.method: a published projection spread evenly across the years

steps: spread it evenly over the years
subtract the accumulated loss from the forecast

assumptions: the published water-supply loss applies directly to access

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: the corrected value is printed, but the translation from supply to access is assumed

strengths: the correction uses a published number rather than a guess
the arithmetic is shown through to 2031
limitations: a supply loss is treated as an equal loss of access
the linearity is assumed, not checked
missing_details: no source year is fixed for the start of the published projection

models.purpose: turn a rise in women's secondary enrollment into a fall in population growth
models.summary: A line fitted on published enrollment and growth data gives the drop in growth that follows a one percent rise in enrollment. That drop is then taken off the growth statistic each year.
